name: Vlad and Trouble at MIT
description: Vladislav has a son who really wanted to go to MIT. The college dormitory at MIT (Moldova Institute of Technology) can be represented as a tree with $$$n$$$ vertices, each vertex being a room with exactly one student. A tree is a connected undirected graph with $$$n$$$ vertices and $$$n-1$$$ edges. Tonight, there are three types of students: students who want to party and play music (marked with $$$\texttt{P}$$$), students who wish to sleep and enjoy silence (marked with $$$\texttt{S}$$$), and students who don't care (marked with $$$\texttt{C}$$$). Initially, all the edges are thin walls which allow music to pass through, so when a partying student puts music on, it will be heard in every room. However, we can place some thick walls on any edges — thick walls don't allow music to pass through them. The university wants to install some thick walls so that every partying student can play music, and no sleepy student can hear it. Because the university lost a lot of money in a naming rights lawsuit, they ask you to find the minimum number of thick walls they will need to use.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 1000$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$) — the number of vertices in the tree. The second line of each test case contains $$$n-1$$$ integers $$$a_2, \dots , a_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq a_i \lt i$$$) — it means there is an edge between $$$i$$$ and $$$a_i$$$ in the tree. The third line of each test case contains a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$ consisting of characters $$$\texttt{P}$$$, $$$\texttt{S}$$$, and $$$\texttt{C}$$$, denoting that student $$$i$$$ is of type $$$s_i$$$. The sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum number of thick walls needed.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1926G — Vlad and Trouble at MIT [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
